title: Quebec party leaders make their pitches as election campaign kicks off | CBC
text:
Quebec party leaders kick off campaigns ahead of Oct. 5 election

Quebec provincial election underway amid U.S. trade war

Quebec election campaign officially begins Thursday. What’s different this time?

What Montreal’s mayor wants to see from the next provincial government

The election period is officially underway and all five leaders of Quebec's main political parties have made their initial pitch.

As leaders tour the province, you can expect them to release their party platforms and announce campaign promises in the coming weeks.

In the meantime, try out CBC's Vote Compass to see which party aligns most with your views.

With the election campaign now underway, Élections Québec says it faces a major challenge: recruiting enough staff to run the polls.

In a statement to CBC News, the agency confirmed it needs to hire and train more than 60,000 people across the province ahead of the advanced polls and Oct. 5 vote.

The agency noted that staffing is an issue leading into every election, adding that an advertising campaign is already underway and applications are open online.

The statement stressed that teenagers aged 16 and 17 are eligible to work during the campaign and can learn more about how elections work in the process.

The leader of the Quebec Liberals stopped for an ice cream in the municipality of Batiscan in the Mauricie region.

He chose a vanilla and chocolate twist. During the stop, a man approached him and said, “Please get rid of Pablo Rodriguez!”

Milliard replied, “I’m the only leader.”

Rodriguez, the former leader of the Quebec Liberals, stepped down last December after controversies involving him and his party.

The PCQ leader had a message to the province's English speakers: "The English community in Quebec has been hostage to the Liberals forever."

Duhaime pointed to polls that suggest the Quebec Liberals have lost popularity among francophones.

He said that hopefully anglophones realize that they would be better off with Conservative MNAs.

The PCQ leader said that in the next few hours he would announce the "greatest" tax reduction.

He also accused Fréchette of instrumentalizing the tariff war during the election and called her a protectionist.

"This election, I want to fight for Quebecers and get more money in their pockets," Duhaime said.

"Quebecers aren't fools. They know our [economic] model is not viable," Duhaime said, noting that the model is at the "end of its rope."

Speaking to Quebecers who are "tired of turning in circles," Duhaime said his party wants to be the "true alternative" to the province's old parties.

He said he wants to remove interprovincial barriers to lessen Quebec's reliance on the United States.

"It's not up to Americans to determine our prosperity. It's up to us. Only us, in Quebec," Duhaime said.

Before Duhaime steps up to the podium, Maïté Blanchette Vézina  —  the Conservatives’ only MNA — took some time to promote her party's ambitions.

"If we're doing politics, it's first and foremost to represent real people," said Blanchette Vézina , who used to be a member of the CAQ.

She said the Conservatives have "pragmatic and courageous" solutions for Quebecers.

The Conservative Party of Quebec leader Éric Duhaime is speaking at a news conference in the riding of Bellechasse, where he is hoping to win a seat.

The party is holding an event that started at 5 p.m. to officially launch the party’s campaign.

During the campaign, the Conservatives will focus on the cost of living, health care, housing and the autonomy of Quebec and its regions.

3 questions with the leader of the Quebec Conservatives

On the first day of the campaign, CBC's Kwabena Oduro caught up and had a brief chat with Éric Duhaime, the leader of the Conservative Party of Quebec.

I just had a quick chat with Éric Duhaime. He says he's feeling confident about his campaign.

Duhaime says his team has been preparing for this for the last four years and he's feeling more ready than he was four years ago.

He is looking to get a seat at the National Assembly for the first time.

He's running in the riding of Bellechasse, just south of Quebec City – one of a few areas where he is hoping his party will make gains.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada outlined her expectations for the next Quebec government at a news conference on Wednesday.

Her requests focus on three key points: homelessness and housing, infrastructure and mobility, and public safety.

She called on the next government to allocate recurring funding for 3,200 emergency shelter spots and to create three centres specializing in mental health and addiction by the summer of 2027.

She reiterated her calls for a REM light-rail train system in the eastern part of the city.

She also called for more funding to help with policing and youth violence prevention.

Last week, Martinez Ferrada announced that she was moving forward with her plan to gradually equip the city's police officers with body cameras.

She also demanded that Quebec change its approach toward Montreal and that the city be consulted before any decision affecting it is made.
